question: Why do surgeons place a surgical drain inside a wound after an operation?

options.A: To keep the patient completely immobile during recovery
options.B: To prevent fluid and blood from collecting inside the wound
options.C: To deliver strong liquid antibiotics directly into tissues
options.D: To speed up the healing of skin stitches

explanation: You've got this! Drains are simply there to stop blood or serum from forming nasty pockets that could lead to an infection. Great clinical thinking! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h1)

question: What is the main goal of using a chest drain to remove air or fluid from the chest cavity?

options.A: It restores negative pressure to help the lung expand properly
options.B: It prevents the patient from coughing up mucus
options.C: It directly cleans the inner lining of the bronchial tubes
options.D: It stops the heart from beating too fast during stress

explanation: Spot on! When air or fluid gets trapped in the chest, it breaks the natural vacuum (negative pressure) and causes the lung to collapse. The chest drain fixes that vacuum. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h1)

question: Which of these is a classic example of an open drainage system?
explanation: A Penrose drain is an open system that lets fluid drain straight onto dressings because it doesn't have a sealed container. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h2)

question: Why do modern surgical wards prefer closed drainage systems over open ones?

options.A: They completely stop the patient from feeling any surgical pain
options.B: They significantly lower the risk of outside bacteria entering the body
options.C: They allow the surgical wound to heal without any dressings at all
options.D: They never require the nurse to empty or measure the collected fluid

explanation: Think of closed systems as sealed packages—because they are closed to the outside air, germs have a much harder time getting in to cause an infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of using a nasogastric (NG) tube for gastric decompression?

options.A: To remove fluid, gas, and contents from the stomach
options.B: To remove blood collections from inside the chest cavity
options.C: To supply oxygen into the upper airway passages
options.D: To drain excess urine directly from the bladder

explanation: Correct! 'Decompression' just means taking the pressure off. An NG tube sucks out built-up gas and fluid so the stomach can rest and the patient won't vomit. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h3)

question: What keeps a Foley urinary catheter securely in place inside the bladder?

options.A: Special surgical glue applied to the inner thigh skin
options.B: A tight plastic clamp attached around the external tubing
options.C: An inflated water balloon near the catheter tip
options.D: Natural suction created by the urine collection bag

explanation: Brilliant! Once the catheter is inside the bladder, we fill a tiny balloon with sterile water so it acts like an anchor and won't slip out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h3)

question: A surgical drain was flowing nicely, but now it has suddenly stopped. What should you suspect first?

options.A: The body has miraculously stopped producing all normal inflammatory fluid
options.B: The collection container is now completely sterile and safe to remove
options.C: The surgical wound has finished healing completely on its own
options.D: The tube might be blocked or kinked inside or outside the patient

explanation: When output stops abruptly, don't assume a miracle healing! Always check the tubing first for a clot, mucus, or a pesky kink. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h4)

question: Which sign around a surgical drain insertion site tells you an infection might be starting?

options.A: Normal skin color with slight firmness around the tube
options.B: Clear pink fluid on a dry, intact outer gauze
options.C: Foul-smelling pus and surrounding skin redness
options.D: A small drop of dried blood near the stitches

explanation: Spot on! Redness, warmth, swelling, and foul-smelling pus are classic signs that bacteria are multiplying. Time to alert the team! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h4)

question: While helping a patient walk, you notice their urine bag is hanging higher than their bladder. Why is this a problem?

options.A: Urine can flow backward into the bladder and cause an infection
options.B: The urine output will instantly turn bright red with blood
options.C: The plastic collection tubing will melt from body heat
options.D: The catheter balloon will automatically pop from the extra pressure

explanation: Gravity works both ways! If the bag is higher than the bladder, contaminated urine can flow right back inside and give the patient a nasty urinary tract infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h5)

question: Why must a nurse use a separate measuring cylinder for each patient when emptying drainage bags?

options.A: To stop the plastic containers from wearing out too quickly
options.B: To prevent cross-contamination and spread of infections between patients
options.C: To make measuring the fluid much faster during busy shifts
options.D: To ensure the hospital records look neat and well-organized

explanation: Infection control 101! Using dedicated equipment for every patient keeps germs from hitching a ride across the ward. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h5)

question: What is your very first action if a surgical drain accidentally falls completely out of a patient's wound?

options.A: Try to gently push the same tube right back into the hole
options.B: Leave the open wound uncovered so fresh air can dry it out
options.C: Cover the open site with a sterile dressing and notify the doctor
options.D: Wash the fallen tube with soap and tape it back onto the skin

explanation: Never try to push a fallen drain back in—that introduces germs! Instead, cover the site with a sterile dressing right away and call the doctor. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h6)

question: When a drainage tube gets blocked, which of these actions is completely WRONG and dangerous?

options.A: Pushing a partially dislodged tube back into the body cavity
options.B: Checking the entire length of the tubing for accidental kinks
options.C: Inspecting the tube for visible blood clots or mucus plugs
options.D: Notifying the medical team if output remains absent

explanation: You got it! Pushing a slipped tube back inside drags surface bacteria straight into sterile tissues. Always check with your senior or doctor first. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h6)

question: Why is a patient told to take a deep breath and hold it while a chest or surgical drain is being removed?

options.A: It increases pressure and prevents air from entering the body cavity
options.B: It completely stops the patient from feeling any discomfort at all
options.C: It relaxes the abdominal muscles so the stitches fall apart
options.D: It forces the remaining fluid to rush out before the hole seals

explanation: Holding the breath creates a little bit of internal pressure, stopping air from being sucked into the empty tract as the tube comes out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h7)

question: What should you do immediately after a drain is successfully pulled out from a surgical wound?

options.A: Ask the patient to stand up and walk around the room
options.B: Leave the small hole open to the air so it dries quickly
options.C: Wash the open tract thoroughly with harsh antiseptic soap
options.D: Apply a sterile, airtight dressing over the insertion site

explanation: Always seal the site immediately with an airtight sterile dressing to protect the healing tissue and stop any air leaks or bleeding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h7)
